conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for taking a few minutes to talk with me. My name is Dr. Morales, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician here. I specialize in caring for new moms during the first year after birth, because this time can bring a lot more ups-and-downs than most people expect.

To get a quick snapshot of how you’re feeling, I’d like to use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS**. It’s just 10 questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team; it won’t go into your general medical record unless you choose to include it.

We’ll go through the questions conversationally, and it usually takes about five minutes. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, just let me know and we can pause or stop.

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?
I’ve still laughed a little—like when my husband sent me that silly meme—but mostly it feels kind of forced. Things that used to crack me up before the baby now just seem… flat, I guess.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I can still laugh sometimes, but it’s not the same. It feels like I have to really force it, and the joy doesn’t last.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I try to tell myself I should be excited about little outings or even just coffee with a friend, but when the time comes it feels like more effort than it’s worth. I still go, and once I’m there I might feel a flicker of enjoyment, but it’s nowhere near the excitement I used to have.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. Like if the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong or I’m not a good mom. Even little things—if I drop a spoon of formula or we’re late for a check-up—I’ll replay it in my head and tell myself I should’ve planned better. It’s not constant, but it happens most days.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s stopped breathing, even though he’s right there looking fine. Or I’ll lie down and picture these awful “what-ifs”—like the stroller rolling into the street or him choking—and I can’t shut the thoughts off for a while. I know they’re probably irrational, but in the moment they feel so real.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes. Sometimes out of nowhere my chest gets tight, my heart races, and I feel like something awful is about to happen even when everything is quiet. It’s only happened a couple of times this week, but each time I had to put the baby in his crib for a minute and go stand by the window, taking deep breaths until the feeling passed.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes. Most days it feels like I’m barely treading water—dishes pile up, the baby needs changing, laundry’s sitting there wet, and I just stare at it feeling paralyzed. I manage to get through the essentials, but it’s like I’m running on empty and any extra little hiccup makes me feel like everything’s about to crash down.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll finally get the baby down, but then I lie there with my mind racing—worrying about SIDS, about whether I’m doing anything right, about how tired I’ll feel tomorrow. It can take me an hour or two to drift off, and even then I wake up a couple of times with those anxious thoughts churning. By morning I feel like I barely slept at all.
I have felt sad or miserable

I feel that way most of the day, pretty much every day. It’s like a heavy cloud that settles in as soon as I open my eyes—this dull sadness that I can’t shake, even when I’m holding the baby and everyone says I should be happy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah, it’s happened twice this week. Yesterday I just sat in the nursery rocker with the baby asleep on my chest and the tears started coming—I couldn’t even name exactly why, just this wave of sadness and exhaustion. And then a few nights ago, after my husband asked how my day was, I burst out crying over nothing specific.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It’s… it’s popped into my head maybe once or twice. Nothing planned, no real urge—just this quick, scary “what if I weren’t here?” kind of thought when everything feels too heavy. I push it away right away, but I hate that it shows up at all.

I hear how heavy life feels right now: the joy that once came easily now seems distant, daily tasks feel overwhelming, and anxious thoughts about your baby race through your mind even when you try to rest. You're working so hard to keep everything afloat, yet you still blame yourself for every tiny hiccup, and tears arrive without warning. The fact that you shared even fleeting thoughts of not wanting to be here tells me how exhausted and stretched you feel, and I want you to know you don't have to carry this weight alone.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to laugh and find joy, describing forced laughter and fleeting joy, aligning with 'definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient reports diminished anticipation and only a "flicker" of enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame occurring "most days" for multiple minor events, aligning with "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, uncontrollable worries about infant safety that feel real in the moment, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic symptoms (tight chest, racing heart, dread) that occur "sometimes" and only twice this week, aligning with the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>"most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption due to racing anxious thoughts, taking 1–2 h to fall asleep and waking multiple times—clearly "most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness that dominates the day, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two clear crying episodes triggered by general overwhelm, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 23 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>; items map onto core <med>DSM-5 criteria</med>: depressed mood most of the day (Q8), markedly diminished interest (Q1-2), guilt/worthlessness (Q3), fatigue (Q6), sleep disturbance (Q7), concentration impacted by worry (Q4-5), and recurrent thoughts of death (Q10). The combination supports likely <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> with comorbid <med>anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> within the next few days
2. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy (CBT or IPT) that specializes in <med>postpartum mood disorders</med>
3. Discuss antidepressant options compatible with breastfeeding if applicable
4. Plan daily 15-minute support check-ins with partner, family, or friend
5. Encourage 20-30 minutes of daylight exposure and gentle movement when possible
6. Limit daily goals to one or two essential tasks; accept help with meals, laundry, night feeds
7. Schedule follow-up EPDS and safety review in 1-2 weeks
8. If thoughts of self-harm intensify, use 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline or go to nearest ER
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note**  

**Reported symptoms:**  
- Persistent low mood and anhedonia most of the day, nearly every day  
- Frequent tearfulness (2 episodes this week)  
- Marked loss of enjoyment/interest in usual activities  
- Excessive or inappropriate guilt and self-blame regarding parenting tasks  
- Daily, distressing, intrusive “what-if” worries about infant safety; occasional panic-type episodes with chest tightness and racing heart  
- Initial and middle insomnia related to racing, anxious thoughts  
- Feeling overwhelmed and “paralyzed” by routine responsibilities  

**Pattern:** Symptoms present most days, interfere with sleep and daily functioning, and have persisted beyond two weeks.  

**Screening significance:**  
- Meets clinical threshold concern for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset (EPDS ≥ probable moderate–severe range)  
- Co-occurring anxiety symptoms (generalized worry and panic-type episodes) requiring further assessment  

**Risk factors:**  
- Sleep disruption linked to mood disturbance  
- Self-reported passive, non-specific thoughts of self-harm (“what if I weren’t here”) without intent or plan; no active suicidal ideation endorsed at present  

**Safety:** No immediate safety concerns identified today; continue to monitor for escalation of self-harm thoughts or development of active suicidal ideation.  

**Recommendation:** Refer for comprehensive diagnostic evaluation and consider evidence-based treatment options (psychotherapy, medication consult, support services).
